name: Maya Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Maya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you tell me is confidential. So feel free to tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a loader underground at the copper mine, eight hundred metres down. It's a big low machine that scoops broken rock at the end of a tunnel and carries it to the ore pass, back and forth, maybe sixty loads a shift. I came to it three years ago from cleaning wards at the hospital, so I'm still the one the shift boss watches on the tight corners.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's good about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Good is the pay, it's nearly double what the hospital gave me, and there's a real crew feeling down there. Hard is the dust and the noise and coming home too tired to help Ana with her maths. Joel drives the town buses, so between his shifts and mine the kids see one of us at a time, never both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, now maybe we can talk about real problems like wages and the dust levels. Online I'd probably share a joke about it. I'm not one for big opinions on the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay about the same for me, and that's fine. The mine already has a few loaders run by remote control from a room on the surface. If that keeps spreading slowly, I'd want to be in that room eventually, but there's no rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, try to get my skills signed off on the bigger loader, and keep paying my union dues. Maybe I'd ask the trainer how people get picked for the remote room. And I'd try to get one month's money saved, because right now we couldn't cover one month if something broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit bored by the whole thing, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the remote room. What do you know about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Dina moved up there last year. She sits in a chair with three screens and runs a loader she can't see except on camera. She says the coffee is better and her lungs feel better, but her back hurts from the chair instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would one month's money in the bank change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop checking the account before I buy groceries. Last winter the car needed a clutch and we put it on the card, and we're still paying for that clutch. One month would mean a clutch is just a bad week, not a bad year.

S0.say: She'd say good, now we can get back to real problems like wages and dust levels. She'd likely share a joke online but not much more.
S0.think: She thinks things stay about the same for her, and that suits her. She would like to move into the remote control room eventually, but sees no rush.
S0.do: Carries on driving and works towards sign-off on the bigger loader. Asks the trainer how people are picked for the remote room, and tries to build one month of savings.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little bored by the subject.
S0.quote: One month would mean a clutch is just a bad week, not a bad year.
S0.fieldNote: Maya's worries in the calm picture are about money and dust, not technology. She already has a clear, modest next step in mind: the remote room her friend moved into. Her steadiness shows in waiting for proof from someone she knows before acting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs to make sure the people underground get first chance at the new jobs on the surface. The company shouldn't be allowed to hire fresh kids for the remote room and push us out. I'd say that at the meeting and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the underground loaders go remote over a few years, and the remote room needs fewer people than the tunnels did. Dina says one person can watch two machines up there. So half of us might not make it up the stairs, and I'm junior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd put my name down for the remote training, and I'd use the AI app on my phone to practise the theory questions, because I'm slow with written tests. I'd go to the union's meetings on the changes and ask questions. And I'd stop the kids' extra activities for a bit and try to save fifty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but not frozen. It's like waiting for exam results.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow with written tests. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I scraped through school and the last test I sat before the mine was a driving test. The loader ticket had a written part and I failed it the first time, then passed it on the second. I'm not stupid, I just freeze when it's a paper in front of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you didn't make it into the remote room, what then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd want the union to make them pay for proper retraining, maybe in maintenance or the processing plant. There's no other mine within two hours, so I can't just walk across the road. Going back to cleaning is possible, but that's half the money and we'd lose the house.

S1.say: She'd say the union must make sure underground workers get first chance at the new surface jobs, instead of the company hiring young people for the remote room.
S1.think: She thinks the loaders go remote over a few years and the control room needs fewer people, perhaps half. As a junior operator, she might not be one of those who make it up.
S1.do: Puts her name down for remote training and uses an AI app on her phone to practise theory questions. Attends union meetings on the changes, pauses the kids' extra activities and tries to save fifty a week.
S1.feel: Nervous but not frozen, like waiting for exam results.
S1.quote: I'm not stupid, I just freeze when it's a paper in front of me.
S1.fieldNote: Maya moves towards the change rather than resisting it, but only along a path she has seen work for a friend. Her fear of written tests is a real barrier she named without prompting. She expects her union to back retraining rather than stop the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government has to step in, full stop. Pay people while it settles, and stop the companies firing everybody in one go. I'd be at the protest with Joel and the kids if there was one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robots can do everything in two years, then the remote room goes too, doesn't it? Dina's chair, my loader, Joel's bus, all of it. That's both of our wages, and we've got less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first week I'd sit down with Joel and go through every bill. We'd stop the card, ask the bank for a mortgage holiday, and apply for any support going the moment it opened. I'd go to every union meeting, and I'd probably ask my mum if the kids could stay with her after school so I could pick up any extra shifts while there are still shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly scared. I'd be lying awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said both your wages. Is that the part that frightens you most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. When the hospital cut hours, Joel's buses kept us going, and when the buses had that strike, my mine pay kept us going. We've always had one leg to stand on. This would be the first time both legs go at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ana and Pip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ana's thirteen, she'd read about it before I could tell her. I'd tell her the truth, that we don't know yet, and that we'll stay together whatever happens. Pip is nine, he'd want to know if he can still have his birthday party, so I'd make sure he can.

S2.say: She'd say it's too fast and the government has to step in to pay people and stop companies firing everyone at once. She'd join a protest with her family.
S2.think: She thinks even the remote room would go, along with her partner's bus job. That means both household wages at once with less than a month saved.
S2.do: Goes through every bill with Joel in the first week, stops the card and asks the bank for a mortgage holiday. Applies for any support as soon as it opens, goes to union meetings and takes extra shifts while they last, with her mother helping with the kids.
S2.feel: Properly scared, lying awake doing sums.
S2.quote: We've always had one leg to stand on. This would be the first time both legs go at once.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hits Maya hardest through her household, not her own job: both incomes are exposed. Her plan is entirely defensive and leans on the union, government support and her mother. She stays practical even when frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, the government and the company both. Start the retraining now, don't wait for the layoffs. I'd say that loud at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough for me to do one proper course, maybe two. Not enough to become a nurse or something like that, but enough to get a ticket for something useful. The hard part is picking the right thing, because I don't know what the robots won't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go up to the remote room as soon as they'd have me, so I'm using the new tools instead of watching them. I'd do a night course in the first year, maybe electrical maintenance, because somebody has to fix the robots for a while at least. We'd try to put away a bit from every payslip, and Joel would look at the training his bus company offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry with a to-do list. That's better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you choose what to retrain in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dina and the electricians at the mine, not a website. I'd probably ask the AI on my phone as well, to compare courses, but I'd trust the people I know more. When I moved from the hospital, it was a guy at the pub who told me the mine was hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut to pay for a night course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our week at Joel's sister's place by the lake, probably for a couple of years. Takeaway Fridays. The kids would moan about the takeaway more than the lake.

S3.say: She'd say five years should be used now by both government and company, with retraining starting before any layoffs.
S3.think: She thinks five years is enough for one or two proper courses but not a whole new career. Her real difficulty is knowing which skills robots won't take.
S3.do: Moves into the remote room as soon as possible and starts a night course, likely electrical maintenance, in the first year. Saves a little from every payslip, cuts the lake trip and takeaway Fridays, and has Joel look at his employer's training.
S3.feel: Worried, but with a to-do list, which feels better.
S3.quote: Worried, but it's a worry with a to-do list. That's better.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Maya shifts from defence to a plan that mixes retraining with staying close to the new machines. She trusts advice from people she knows over websites, though she'd use AI to compare options. The time buys her a sense of control, not safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it, and a disgrace if we waste it. The union should be setting up training with the company now. I'd also say the profits from the robots have to be shared with the towns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years takes me to fifty-three with the kids through school. I think I could actually get a proper trade in that time, or work up in the remote room and then into supervising the robots. It still ends in the same place, but I might get to choose my door instead of being pushed through one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the remote room and an electrical certificate over the first two or three years, paid for by the company if the union can win it. I'd learn the AI tools properly, not just my phone, because whatever I end up doing will have them in it. We'd save steadily and maybe pay a chunk off the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly I feel like I could get somewhere. It's the first one that doesn't make my stomach drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Ana and Pip in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Ana to finish school knowing how to work with these machines, not be scared of them like I was. Pip loves building things, maybe he goes into a trade. I don't want them underground, I'll say that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's a gift if used. What would wasting it look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company waiting until year nine and then sending letters. The government holding inquiries for eight years. Me telling myself I'll start the course next year, every year, which I know I'm capable of.

S4.say: She'd call ten years a gift if used and a disgrace if wasted. She'd push the union to set up training now and argue that robot profits be shared with mining towns.
S4.think: She thinks a decade could let her gain a trade or move through the remote room into supervising machines. The ending is the same, but she might choose her own path.
S4.do: Moves to the remote room and earns an electrical certificate over the first two or three years, ideally paid for by the company through a union deal. Learns AI tools properly, saves steadily and pays down part of the mortgage.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but hopeful that she could get somewhere.
S4.quote: It still ends in the same place, but I might get to choose my door instead of being pushed through one.
S4.fieldNote: The decade is where Maya's steadiness pays off: she sees a sequence of proven steps and is willing to take them. She is candid that her own delay is a risk. Her politics show in wanting gains shared with towns, not in opposing the change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it takes Joel's bus and my loader at the same time and we'd have no cushion at all. What would help is income support that arrives straight away, not in six months, and retraining that the company pays for. And a pause on mortgage payments for families where both people lose work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the women underground. There are only six of us on my level, and we fought to get those jobs. I'd hate for the robots to arrive just as we finally got a foot in the door.

headlineQuote: I'd hate for the robots to arrive just as we finally got a foot in the door.
portrait: Maya Wagner is a 43-year-old underground loader operator at a large copper mine, three years in after leaving a hospital cleaning job for better pay. She and her partner Joel, a bus driver, have two children and almost no savings. She is pro-union and practical, willing to change once she's seen it work for someone she knows, like her friend in the remote control room. The slow pictures barely trouble her, but the two-year AGI picture alarms her because it threatens both household incomes at once. With more warning she plans step by step: the remote room, an electrical course and steady saving.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it would take both her job and Joel's at once with no savings to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: Immediate income support, company-paid retraining and a pause on mortgage payments for families where both earners lose work.
